stem.en: Why can an insect-pollinated plant form seeds with far fewer pollen grains than a wind-pollinated grass?

text.en: Its seeds form without any need for pollen

feedback.en: Every seed here needs pollination. This plant simply loses fewer grains on the way.

text.en: An insect takes its grains to other flowers

feedback.en: Yes. Grains stick to the insect, which then lands on other flowers.

text.en: Wind cannot lift the pollen of a grass plant

feedback.en: Wind does carry grass pollen. Its grains are light and small.

text.en: Its flowers are always far bigger than the insects

feedback.en: Flower size is not the reason. What matters is how the grains travel.

explanation.en: Sticky or spiny grains attach to an insect, and the insect visits other flowers, so many grains reach a stigma. Wind carries grains in all directions, so most are lost.

hints.en: Where does each grain end up?
Who visits flowers, and who just blows past?
